questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}-6xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=4x-6y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4x-6y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=-6x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4y & 4x-6y \\ 4x-6y & -6x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=4\cdot (-6)-(-2)\cdot (-2)=-28.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{xy})={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} & {e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {e}^{xy}(1+xy) & {x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=exy.

a
[x2exyexy(2+xy)exy(2+xy)y2exy]
b
[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy]
c
[exyexy+xyexy+xyexy]
d
[exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)exy]
e
[y2exyexyexyx2exy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(exy)∂∂y(exy)]=[yexyxexy]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(yexy)=y2exy∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(yexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xexy)=x2exy

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy].

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=y2(x2−1).

a
[2y002(x2−1)]
b
[22y2y2(x2−1)]
c
[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)]
d
[2y2xy2xy2(x2−1)]
e
[2y2x2x2(x2−1)]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(y2(x2−1))∂∂y(y2(x2−1))]=[2xy22y(x2−1)]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy2)=2y2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2y(x2−1))=4xy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy2)=4xy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2y(x2−1))=2(x2−1)

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y.$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=xln⁡y−y.

a
[0xyxy−1y2]
b
[01y1y−xy2]
c
[1xyxy−x2y2]
d
[−xy2xyxy0]
e
[01y21y2−xy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(xln⁡y−y)∂∂y(xln⁡y−y)]=[ln⁡yxy−1]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(ln⁡y)=0∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xy−1)=1y∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(ln⁡y)=1y∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xy−1)=−xy2

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[01y1y−xy2].

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$

{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}-6xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=4x-6y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4x-6y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=-6x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4y & 4x-6y \\ 4x-6y & -6x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=4\cdot (-6)-(-2)\cdot (-2)=-28.
$$

Question 5
?

Given that f′(x,y)=[4xy−3y22x2−6xy], evaluate the Hessian determinant of f(x,y) at the point (1,1).

a
25
b
−40
c
−16
d
32
e
−28
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn), the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

The Hessian determinant H(x,y) is the determinant of the second derivative: H(x)=det(f″(x))

In our case, we have f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, notice that since f′(x,y)=[4xy−3y22x2−6xy], we must have ∂f∂x=4xy−3y2,∂f∂y=2x2−6xy.

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: ∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(4xy−3y2)=4y∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2x2−6xy)=4x−6y∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(4xy−3y2)=4x−6y∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2x2−6xy)=−6x

So, the second derivative is f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[4y4x−6y4x−6y−6x].

Evaluating the second derivative at (1,1), we obtain f″(1,1)=[4−2−2−6].

Finally, we have H(1,1)=4⋅(−6)−(−2)⋅(−2)=−28.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}.$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{xy})={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} & {e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {e}^{xy}(1+xy) & {x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=exy.

a
[x2exyexy(2+xy)exy(2+xy)y2exy]
b
[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy]
c
[exyexy+xyexy+xyexy]
d
[exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)exy]
e
[y2exyexyexyx2exy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(exy)∂∂y(exy)]=[yexyxexy]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(yexy)=y2exy∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(yexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xexy)=x2exy

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy].

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{xy})={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} & {e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {e}^{xy}(1+xy) & {x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}.$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{xy})={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} & {e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {e}^{xy}(1+xy) & {x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=exy.

a
[x2exyexy(2+xy)exy(2+xy)y2exy]
b
[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy]
c
[exyexy+xyexy+xyexy]
d
[exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)exy]
e
[y2exyexyexyx2exy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(exy)∂∂y(exy)]=[yexyxexy]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(yexy)=y2exy∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(yexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xexy)=x2exy

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy].

solution.reasoning: The second derivative is the Hessian. Since f_x=ye^{xy} and f_y=xe^{xy}, we have f_{xx}=y^2e^{xy}, f_{yy}=x^2e^{xy}, and f_{xy}=f_{yx}=e^{xy}(1+xy). Thus option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{xy})={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} & {e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {e}^{xy}(1+xy) & {x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=exy.

a
[x2exyexy(2+xy)exy(2+xy)y2exy]
b
[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy]
c
[exyexy+xyexy+xyexy]
d
[exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)exy]
e
[y2exyexyexyx2exy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(exy)∂∂y(exy)]=[yexyxexy]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(yexy)=y2exy∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(yexy)=exy+xy exy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xexy)=x2exy

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[y2exyexy(1+xy)exy(1+xy)x2exy].

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1).$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=y2(x2−1).

a
[2y002(x2−1)]
b
[22y2y2(x2−1)]
c
[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)]
d
[2y2xy2xy2(x2−1)]
e
[2y2x2x2(x2−1)]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(y2(x2−1))∂∂y(y2(x2−1))]=[2xy22y(x2−1)]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy2)=2y2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2y(x2−1))=4xy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy2)=4xy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2y(x2−1))=2(x2−1)

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)].

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1).$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=y2(x2−1).

a
[2y002(x2−1)]
b
[22y2y2(x2−1)]
c
[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)]
d
[2y2xy2xy2(x2−1)]
e
[2y2x2x2(x2−1)]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(y2(x2−1))∂∂y(y2(x2−1))]=[2xy22y(x2−1)]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy2)=2y2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2y(x2−1))=4xy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy2)=4xy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2y(x2−1))=2(x2−1)

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)].

solution.reasoning: The second derivative is the Hessian. Differentiating gives f_x=2xy^2 and f_y=2y(x^2-1), so f_{xx}=2y^2, f_{xy}=f_{yx}=4xy, and f_{yy}=2(x^2-1). Therefore option c is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=y2(x2−1).

a
[2y002(x2−1)]
b
[22y2y2(x2−1)]
c
[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)]
d
[2y2xy2xy2(x2−1)]
e
[2y2x2x2(x2−1)]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(y2(x2−1))∂∂y(y2(x2−1))]=[2xy22y(x2−1)]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy2)=2y2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2y(x2−1))=4xy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy2)=4xy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2y(x2−1))=2(x2−1)

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[2y24xy4xy2(x2−1)].

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y.$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=xln⁡y−y.

a
[0xyxy−1y2]
b
[01y1y−xy2]
c
[1xyxy−x2y2]
d
[−xy2xyxy0]
e
[01y21y2−xy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(xln⁡y−y)∂∂y(xln⁡y−y)]=[ln⁡yxy−1]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(ln⁡y)=0∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xy−1)=1y∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(ln⁡y)=1y∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xy−1)=−xy2

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[01y1y−xy2].

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=xln⁡y−y.

a
[0xyxy−1y2]
b
[01y1y−xy2]
c
[1xyxy−x2y2]
d
[−xy2xyxy0]
e
[01y21y2−xy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(xln⁡y−y)∂∂y(xln⁡y−y)]=[ln⁡yxy−1]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(ln⁡y)=0∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xy−1)=1y∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(ln⁡y)=1y∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xy−1)=−xy2

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[01y1y−xy2].

solution.reasoning: For y>0, f_x=\ln y and f_y=x/y-1. Thus f_{xx}=0, f_{xy}=f_{yx}=1/y, and f_{yy}=-x/y^2. The Hessian matches option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem: Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y.$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find f″(x,y) for the function f(x,y)=xln⁡y−y.

a
[0xyxy−1y2]
b
[01y1y−xy2]
c
[1xyxy−x2y2]
d
[−xy2xyxy0]
e
[01y21y2−xy]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, we compute the first derivative of f(x,y), as follows:

f′(x,y)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y]=[∂∂x(xln⁡y−y)∂∂y(xln⁡y−y)]=[ln⁡yxy−1]

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(ln⁡y)=0∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(xy−1)=1y∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(ln⁡y)=1y∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(xy−1)=−xy2

So, the second derivative is

f″(x,y)=[01y1y−xy2].

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,-1).$
question.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$

?

Given that f′(x,y)=[2xy2−2x2yx2], evaluate the Hessian determinant of f(x,y) at the point (1,−1).

a
−16
b
−8
c
16
d
8
e
−24
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

The Hessian determinant H(x,y) is the determinant of the second derivative:

H(x)=det(f″(x))

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, notice that since f′(x,y)=[2xy2−2x2yx2], we must have ∂f∂x=2xy2−2x,∂f∂y=2yx2.

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: ∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy2−2x)=2y2−2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2yx2)=4xy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy2−2x)=4xy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2yx2)=2x2

So, the second derivative is f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[2y2−24xy4xy2x2].

Evaluating the second derivative at (1,−1), we obtain f″(1,−1)=[0−4−42].

Finally, we have H(1,−1)=0⋅2−(−4)⋅(−4)=−16.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$

Question 4
?

Given that f′(x,y)=[2xy2−2x2yx2], evaluate the Hessian determinant of f(x,y) at the point (1,−1).

a
−16
b
−8
c
16
d
8
e
−24
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn),

the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix

f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

The Hessian determinant H(x,y) is the determinant of the second derivative:

H(x)=det(f″(x))

In our case, we have

f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, notice that since f′(x,y)=[2xy2−2x2yx2], we must have ∂f∂x=2xy2−2x,∂f∂y=2yx2.

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: ∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(2xy2−2x)=2y2−2∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2yx2)=4xy∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(2xy2−2x)=4xy∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2yx2)=2x2

So, the second derivative is f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[2y2−24xy4xy2x2].

Evaluating the second derivative at (1,−1), we obtain f″(1,−1)=[0−4−42].

Finally, we have H(1,−1)=0⋅2−(−4)⋅(−4)=−16.

solution.reasoning: Differentiating the gradient gives f_{xx}=2y^2-2, f_{xy}=f_{yx}=4xy, and f_{yy}=2x^2. At (1,-1), the Hessian is [[0,-4],[-4,2]], whose determinant is 0·2-(-4)^2=-16. Option a is mathematically correct; no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}-6xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=4x-6y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4x-6y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=-6x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4y & 4x-6y \\ 4x-6y & -6x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=4\cdot (-6)-(-2)\cdot (-2)=-28.
$$

Question 5
?

Given that f′(x,y)=[4xy−3y22x2−6xy], evaluate the Hessian determinant of f(x,y) at the point (1,1).

a
25
b
−40
c
−16
d
32
e
−28
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a function f:Rn→R, given by f:[x1x2⋮xn]⏟x⟶f(x1,x2,…,xn), the second derivative of f is given by the n×n matrix f″(x)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2].

The Hessian determinant H(x,y) is the determinant of the second derivative: H(x)=det(f″(x))

In our case, we have f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2].

First, notice that since f′(x,y)=[4xy−3y22x2−6xy], we must have ∂f∂x=4xy−3y2,∂f∂y=2x2−6xy.

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: ∂2f∂x2=∂∂x(4xy−3y2)=4y∂2f∂x∂y=∂∂x(2x2−6xy)=4x−6y∂2f∂y∂x=∂∂y(4xy−3y2)=4x−6y∂2f∂y2=∂∂y(2x2−6xy)=−6x

So, the second derivative is f″(x,y)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]=[4y4x−6y4x−6y−6x].

Evaluating the second derivative at (1,1), we obtain f″(1,1)=[4−2−2−6].

Finally, we have H(1,1)=4⋅(−6)−(−2)⋅(−2)=−28.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}cxy,\, & 0\le x\le y<1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
questions.worked_solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y<1\}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/01f3a8d99dd38ce2a728fe2cb4e4ab8de933ccd9ba27c87174779c428c303f48.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[cx\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=x}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{c{x}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{c{x}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{c{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{c{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{4}-\frac{c}{8} \\  & =\frac{c}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{8}=1\,⇒\,c=8.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}c{x}^{2}y,\, & {x}^{2}\le y<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
questions.worked_solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y<1\}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/b9cfac7f0f82088900ab5e603588a73d4932f08f592321c797a1fd94b8bafb4e.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[c{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[c(\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{7}}{14})]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4c}{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{4c}{21}=1\,⇒\,c=\frac{21}{4}.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y),\, & 0\le x\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X\le \frac{\pi }{4}).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}\},$ and the event $A=\{X\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/ea585fb6e12672f5cc854578cb12ff0357cfcd8d2f3d3b75a82723241cdaf3d4.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le \frac{\pi }{4}) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{x}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[{\int }_{x}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=x}^{y=\pi /2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0+1 \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & ≈0.793.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2},\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X>1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=[0,2]\times [0,1],$ and the event $A=\{X>1\}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/26cbd44827c3a5a3fde5d61b631ce4f214bcf9a36ce6bf76129b1fe9f9478eff.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>1) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{A}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{Area}(A) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
5.Computing a Probability Using a Joint PDF?

The random variables X and Y have the joint probability density function f(x,y)={12,0≤x≤2,0≤y≤1,0,otherwise.

Find P(X>Y).

E

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y<1\}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/01f3a8d99dd38ce2a728fe2cb4e4ab8de933ccd9ba27c87174779c428c303f48.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[cx\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=x}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{c{x}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{c{x}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{c{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{c{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{4}-\frac{c}{8} \\  & =\frac{c}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{8}=1\,⇒\,c=8.
$$

To verify that f(x,y) is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

  • f(x,y)≥0 for all (x,y)∈R2

  • ∬R2f(x,y)dxdy=1

First, let's sketch the region D={(x,y):0≤x≤y<1}.

Now, let's check our conditions:

  • For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have ∬R2f(x,y)dxdy=∬Df(x,y)dxdy=∫01∫x1cxydydx=1. c8=1⇒c=8.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}cxy,\, & 0\le x\le y<1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
question.worked_solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le y<1\}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/01f3a8d99dd38ce2a728fe2cb4e4ab8de933ccd9ba27c87174779c428c303f48.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{1}cxy\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[cx\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=x}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{c{x}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{c{x}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{c{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{c{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{c}{4}-\frac{c}{8} \\  & =\frac{c}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{c}{8}=1\,⇒\,c=8.
$$

Question 1
?

The random variables X and Y have the joint probability density function f(x,y)={cxy,0≤x≤y<1,0,otherwise where c is a positive real number. Find the value of c.

a
18
b
2
c
8
d
4
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To verify that f(x,y) is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

  • f(x,y)≥0 for all (x,y)∈R2

  • ∬R2f(x,y)dxdy=1

First, let's sketch the region D={(x,y):0≤x≤y<1}.

Now, let's check our conditions:

  • Since c>0, we clearly have f(x,y)≥0 for all (x,y)∈R2. So the first condition is satisfied.

  • For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have ∬R2f(x,y)dxdy=∬Df(x,y)dxdy=∫01∫x1cxydydx=1. We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to y, treating x as a constant: ∫01[∫x1cxydy]dx=∫01[cx⋅y22]y=xy=1dx=∫01(cx2−cx32)dx Then, we integrate with respect to x: ∫01(cx2−cx32)dx=[cx24−cx48]01=c4−c8=c8

Hence,

c8=1⇒c=8.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}c{x}^{2}y,\, & {x}^{2}\le y<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
question.worked_solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y<1\}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/b9cfac7f0f82088900ab5e603588a73d4932f08f592321c797a1fd94b8bafb4e.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[c{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[c(\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{7}}{14})]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4c}{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{4c}{21}=1\,⇒\,c=\frac{21}{4}.
$$

Question 2
?

The random variables X and Y have the joint probability density function f(x,y)={cx2y,x2≤y<1,0,otherwise where c is a positive real number. Find the value of c.

a
421
b
212
c
14
d
114
e
214
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To verify that f(x,y) is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

  • f(x,y)≥0 for all (x,y)∈R2

  • ∬R2f(x,y)dxdy=1

First, let's sketch the region D={(x,y):x2≤y<1}.

Now, let's check our conditions:

  • Since c>0, we clearly have f(x,y)≥0 for all (x,y)∈R2. So the first condition is satisfied.

  • For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have ∬R2f(x,y)dxdy=∬Df(x,y)dxdy=∫−11∫x21cx2ydydx=1. We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to y, treating x as a constant: ∫−11∫x21cx2ydydx=∫−11[cx2⋅y22]y=x2y=1dx=∫−11cx2(1−x42)dx Then, we integrate with respect to x: ∫−11cx2(1−x42)dx=[c(x36−x714)]−11=4c21

Hence,

4c21=1⇒c=214.

solution.reasoning: The support includes negative x: for 0≤y<1, −√y≤x≤√y. Normalization gives 1=\int_0^1\int_{-\sqrt{y}}^{\sqrt{y}}cx^2y\,dx\,dy=(2c/3)\int_0^1y^{5/2}\,dy=4c/21. Thus c=21/4, option e. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}c{x}^{2}y,\, & {x}^{2}\le y<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $c$ is a positive real number. Find the value of $c.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y<1\}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/b9cfac7f0f82088900ab5e603588a73d4932f08f592321c797a1fd94b8bafb4e.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating  $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}c{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[c{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}c{x}^{2}(\frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2})\,\text{d}x & ={[c(\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{7}}{14})]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4c}{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{4c}{21}=1\,⇒\,c=\frac{21}{4}.
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y),\, & 0\le x\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X\le \frac{\pi }{4}).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}\},$ and the event $A=\{X\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/ea585fb6e12672f5cc854578cb12ff0357cfcd8d2f3d3b75a82723241cdaf3d4.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le \frac{\pi }{4}) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{x}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[{\int }_{x}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=x}^{y=\pi /2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0+1 \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & ≈0.793.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}\},$ and the event $A=\{X\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/ea585fb6e12672f5cc854578cb12ff0357cfcd8d2f3d3b75a82723241cdaf3d4.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le \frac{\pi }{4}) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{x}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[{\int }_{x}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=x}^{y=\pi /2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2}))\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0+1 \\  & =\frac{3-\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & ≈0.793.\end{aligned}
$$

The random variables X and Y have the joint probability density function f(x,y)={sin⁡(x+y),0≤x≤y≤π2,0,otherwise.

Find P(X≤π4). Round your answer to 3 decimal places.

a
 0.793
b
 0.548
c
 0.417
d
 0.827
e
 0.613
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If f(x,y) is a joint probability density function for the random variables X and Y and A⊂R2, then

P((X,Y)∈A)=∬Af(x,y)dxdy.

Notice that f(x,y) is nonnegative in the region D={(x,y):0≤y≤x≤π2}, and the event A={X≤π4} corresponds to a subset of D, shown as the shaded region below:

Therefore,

P(X≤π4)=∬Af(x,y)dydx=∫0π/4∫xπ/2sin⁡(x+y)dydx=∫0π/4[∫xπ/2sin⁡(x+y)dy]dx=∫0π/4[−cos⁡(x+y)]y=xy=π/2dx=∫0π/4(cos⁡(2x)−cos⁡(x+π2))dx=[12sin⁡(2x)−sin⁡(x+π2)]0π/4=12−22−0+1=3−22≈0.793.

The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2},\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

If f(x,y) is a joint probability density function for the random variables X and Y and A⊂R2, then

P((X,Y)∈A)=∬Af(x,y)dxdy.

Notice that f(x,y) is nonnegative in the region D=[0,2]×[0,1], and the event A={X>1} corresponds to a subset of D, shown as the shaded region below:

P(X>1)=∬Af(x,y)dxdy=∬A12dxdy=12Area(A)=12.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=[0,2]\times [0,1],$ and the event $A=\{X>1\}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/26cbd44827c3a5a3fde5d61b631ce4f214bcf9a36ce6bf76129b1fe9f9478eff.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>1) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{A}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{Area}(A) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2},\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X>Y).$
question.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=[0,2]\times [0,1],$ and the event $A=\{X>Y\}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215348/assets/2db85950b4d45901d79c173f264173d0c38046b2f087d0a28c8d5c69f024e31f.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>Y) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{A}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{Area}(A) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
