questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ |

Find $\text{Var}[2X+3Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ | $0.8$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =0.8-{0.8}^{2} \\  & =0.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.6 \\  & =1.6\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.6}^{2} \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We compute $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+1\cdot 1\cdot f(1,1)+1\cdot 2\cdot f(1,2) \\  & =0+0+1\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.3-0.8\cdot 1.6 \\  & =0.02.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X-Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.7 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =0.84.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =0.5-{0.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+2\cdot 0\cdot f(2,0)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1) \\  & =0+0+0+2\cdot 0.3 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.6-1.4\cdot 0.5 \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.84+(-1)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-1)\cdot (-0.1) \\  & =7.56+0.25+0.6 \\  & =8.41.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X+4Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ | $0.55$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.45+4\cdot 0.55 \\  & =2.2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.45+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.55 \\  & =8.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =8.8-{2.2}^{2} \\  & =3.96.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+4\cdot 1\cdot f(4,1)+4\cdot 2\cdot f(4,2) \\  & =0+0+4\cdot 0.2+8\cdot 0.35 \\  & =3.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =3.6-2.2\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X+4Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3.96+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =35.64+4+7.2 \\  & =46.84.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Consider two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\text{E}[X]=2,$ $\text{E}[Y]=4,$ mixed moment $\text{E}[XY]=10,$ and second raw moments $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=9$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=20.$ Find the variance of $2X-5Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =9-{2}^{2} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =20-{4}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =10-2\cdot 4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X-5Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 5+(-5)^{2}\cdot 4+2\cdot 2\cdot (-5)\cdot 2 \\  & =20+100-40 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X-2Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.55+2\cdot 0.45 \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.55+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.45 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =1.8-{0.9}^{2} \\  & =0.99.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1)+2\cdot 2\cdot f(2,2) \\  & =0+0+2\cdot 0.2+4\cdot 0.25 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.4-0.9\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.99+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-2)\cdot 0.05 \\  & =8.91+1-0.6 \\  & =9.31.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
For three random variables ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3},$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]=3,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]=0.5,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{3}]=1.5\,
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=-0.75,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]=-3.5,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=4\,
$$

Find $\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}+6{X}_{3}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}+6{X}_{3}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot 3+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{6}^{2}\cdot 1.5 \\  & +2\cdot 1\cdot 4\cdot (-0.75)+2\cdot 1\cdot 6\cdot (-3.5)+2\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdot 4 \\  & =3+8+54-6-42+192 \\  & =209.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
For three random variables ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3},$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]=5,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]=4,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{3}]=2\,
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=3,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]=1,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=2\,
$$

Find $\text{Var}[3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3}] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 5+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+{4}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & +2\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 3+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =45+16+32+36+24+32 \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Variance of a Sum or Difference of Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\textrm{Var}[X] = 3,$ $\textrm{Var}[Y] = 0.24,$ and $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 0.2.$ Determine $\textrm{Var}[X-Y].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[X \pm Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] \pm 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\textrm{Var}[X - Y] = 3 + 0.24 - 2 \cdot 0.2 = 2.84.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\textrm{Var}[X] = 5,$ $\textrm{Var}[Y] = 2,$ and $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 3.$ Find $\textrm{Var}[2X - 5Y].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X] + b^2\textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab\,\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X-5Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 5+(-5)^{2}\cdot 2+2\cdot 2\cdot (-5)\cdot 3 \\  & =20+50-60 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ |

Find $\textrm{Var}[5X+2Y].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab\,\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2,
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ |
| $f_Y$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\textrm{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space $S_X,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.6 \\  & =1.8\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =5.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5.4-{1.8}^{2} \\  & =2.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space $S_Y,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2-{1}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\textrm{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+3\cdot 0\cdot f(3,0)+3\cdot 2\cdot f(3,2) \\  & =0+0+0+6\cdot 0.2 \\  & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.2-1.8\cdot 1 \\  & =-0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X+2Y] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 2.16+{2}^{2}\cdot 1+2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot (-0.6) \\  & =54+4-12 \\  & =46.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Combined Variance Given Some Moments

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Three Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem:
For three random variables $X_1,X_2,$ and $X_3,$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X_1] = 1,   \qquad
\textrm{Var}[X_2] = 3,   \qquad
\textrm{Var}[X_3] = 8   \qquad
$$

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2] = 2,   \qquad
\textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_3] = 4,   \qquad
\textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_3] = -5   \qquad
$$

Find $\textrm{Var}[5X_1 + 2X_2 + 3X_3].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ are random variables, and $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}\left[\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i X_i \right]
= \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \textrm{Var}[X_i] + 2\sum\limits_{i <     j} a_i a_j \textrm{Cov}[X_i,X_j].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+3{X}_{3}] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 1+{2}^{2}\cdot 3+{3}^{2}\cdot 8 \\  & +2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot 2+2\cdot 5\cdot 3\cdot 4+2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot (-5) \\  & =25+12+72+40+120-60 \\  & =209.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Proof of the Sum Formula
tutorials.problem:
Let's prove the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X+ Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]
$$

Applying the definition of variance and using the linearity of expectation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[((X+Y)-\text{E}[X+Y])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[((X-\text{E}[X])+(Y-\text{E}[Y]))^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])].\end{aligned}
$$

Distributing the expected value, and using the fact that $\textrm{E}[aX] = a\cdot \textrm{E}[X]$ for constant $a,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}]+\text{E}[(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}]+2\cdot \text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]+2\text{Cov}[X,Y]\end{aligned}
$$

as required. 

The proof for the difference between two random variables is similar.

tutorial.name: The Variance of a Sum of Scaled Random Variables
tutorial.problem:
If $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab \textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 0,$ and we recover the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] .
$$

Question 10
?

For two random variables X and Y, we have Var[X]=0.24, Var[Y]=0.06, and Cov[X,Y]=0.08. Find Var[2X−8Y].

a
2.53
b
1.78
c
2.24
d
1.18
e
1.51
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X and Y are random variables, and a and b are constants, then Var[aX+bY]=a2Var[X]+b2Var[Y]+2abCov[X,Y].

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain Var[2X−8Y]=22⋅0.24+(−8)2⋅0.06+2⋅2⋅(−8)⋅0.08=0.96+3.84−2.56=2.24.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Scaled Random Variables
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab\,\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2,
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ |
| $f_Y$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\textrm{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space $S_X,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.6 \\  & =1.8\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =5.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5.4-{1.8}^{2} \\  & =2.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space $S_Y,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2-{1}^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\textrm{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+3\cdot 0\cdot f(3,0)+3\cdot 2\cdot f(3,2) \\  & =0+0+0+6\cdot 0.2 \\  & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.2-1.8\cdot 1 \\  & =-0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X+2Y] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 2.16+{2}^{2}\cdot 1+2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot (-0.6) \\  & =54+4-12 \\  & =46.\end{aligned}
$$

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =8.8-{2.2}^{2} \\  & =3.96.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =9-{2}^{2} \\  & =5\end{aligned}

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =20-{4}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.55+2\cdot 0.45 \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.55+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.45 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =1.8-{0.9}^{2} \\  & =0.99.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1)+2\cdot 2\cdot f(2,2) \\  & =0+0+2\cdot 0.2+4\cdot 0.25 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.4-0.9\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.99+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-2)\cdot 0.05 \\  & =8.91+1-0.6 \\  & =9.31.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\textrm{Var} \left[ \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i X_i \right] = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \textrm{Var}[X_i] + 2\sum\limits_{i < j} a_i a_j \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j]
$$

Let's see an example of how this works in practice.

\textrm{Var}\left[\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i X_i \right]
= \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \textrm{Var}[X_i] + 2\sum\limits_{i <     j} a_i a_j \textrm{Cov}[X_i,X_j].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$

$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+3{X}_{3}] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 1+{2}^{2}\cdot 3+{3}^{2}\cdot 8 \\  & +2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot 2+2\cdot 5\cdot 3\cdot 4+2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot (-5) \\  & =25+12+72+40+120-60 \\  & =209.\end{aligned}

Find Var[X1+4X2+6X3].

tutorial.name: Proof of the Sum Formula
tutorial.problem:
Let's prove the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X+ Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]
$$

Applying the definition of variance and using the linearity of expectation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[((X+Y)-\text{E}[X+Y])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[((X-\text{E}[X])+(Y-\text{E}[Y]))^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])].\end{aligned}
$$

Distributing the expected value, and using the fact that $\textrm{E}[aX] = a\cdot \textrm{E}[X]$ for constant $a,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}]+\text{E}[(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}]+2\cdot \text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]+2\text{Cov}[X,Y]\end{aligned}
$$

as required. 

The proof for the difference between two random variables is similar.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=0.64,$ $\text{Var}[Y]=2.56,$ and $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.48.$ Find $\text{Var}[X+Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, then

$$
\text{Var}[X\pm Y]=\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]\pm 2\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\text{Var}[X+Y]=0.64+2.56+2\cdot 0.48=4.16.
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, then

$$
\text{Var}[X\pm Y]=\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]\pm 2\text{Cov}[X,Y].

\text{Var}[X-Y]=\frac{7}{4}+\frac{5}{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{4}=\frac{11}{4}.
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=7,$ $\text{Var}[Y]=5,$ and $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=3.$ Find $\text{Var}[X+Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, then

$$
\text{Var}[X\pm Y]=\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]\pm 2\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\text{Var}[X+Y]=7+5+2\cdot 3=18.
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=\frac{1}{8},$ $\text{Var}[Y]=\frac{3}{4},$ and $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\frac{5}{16}.$ Find $\text{Var}[X+Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, then

$$
\text{Var}[X\pm Y]=\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]\pm 2\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

$$
\text{Var}[X+Y]=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{3}{4}+2\cdot \frac{5}{16}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

For two random variables X and Y, we have Var[X]=18, Var[Y]=34, and Cov[X,Y]=516. Find Var[X+Y].

a
1916
b
32
c
98
d
118
e
54
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X and Y are random variables, then Var[X±Y]=Var[X]+Var[Y]±2Cov[X,Y].

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain Var[X+Y]=18+34+2⋅516=32.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Variance of a Sum or Difference of Random Variables

solution.reasoning: Applying the variance identity gives Var[X+Y] = 1/8 + 3/4 + 2(5/16) = 3/2, option b. However, the premises are inconsistent: Cov[X,Y]^2 = 25/256 exceeds Var[X]Var[Y] = 24/256, violating the covariance inequality. Thus 3/2 is the intended algebraic response, but no such random variables exist. Math Academy's current answer key is not captured.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=2,$ $\text{Var}[Y]=4,$ and $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=3.$ Find $\text{Var}[X+2Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+2Y] & ={1}^{2}\cdot 2+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+2\cdot 1\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\  & =2+16+12 \\  & =30.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=0.24,$ $\text{Var}[Y]=0.06,$ and $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.08.$ Find $\text{Var}[2X-8Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X-8Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 0.24+(-8)^{2}\cdot 0.06+2\cdot 2\cdot (-8)\cdot 0.08 \\  & =0.96+3.84-2.56 \\  & =2.24.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ |

Find $\text{Var}[2X+3Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ | $0.8$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =0.8-{0.8}^{2} \\  & =0.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.6 \\  & =1.6\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.6}^{2} \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We compute $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+1\cdot 1\cdot f(1,1)+1\cdot 2\cdot f(1,2) \\  & =0+0+1\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.3-0.8\cdot 1.6 \\  & =0.02.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X+3Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 0.16+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.24+2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 0.02 \\  & =0.64+2.16+0.24 \\  & =3.04.\end{aligned}
$$

f Y=1 Y=2
X=0 0.1 0.1
X=1 0.3 0.5

Find Var[2X+3Y].

a
1.82
b
1.44
c
2.96
d
3.04
e
3.16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X and Y are random variables and a and b are constants, then

Var[aX+bY]=a2Var[X]+b2Var[Y]+2abCov[X,Y].

Also, the variance of a random variable X is determined by the formula

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2,

and the covariance of two random variables X and Y is given by the formula

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y].

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for X and Y. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

f Y=1 Y=2 fX
X=0 0.1 0.1 0.2
X=1 0.3 0.5 0.8
fY 0.4 0.6 1

Now, we can find Var[X]. If X is defined on a sample space SX, then

E[X]=∑x∈SXx⋅fX(x)=0⋅0.2+1⋅0.8=0.8

and

E[X2]=∑x∈SXx2⋅fX(x)=02⋅0.2+12⋅0.8=0.8.

Therefore,

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2=0.8−0.82=0.16.

Similarly, if Y is defined on a sample space SY, then

E[Y]=∑y∈Syy⋅fY(y)=1⋅0.4+2⋅0.6=1.6

and

E[Y2]=∑y∈Syy2⋅fY(y)=12⋅0.4+22⋅0.6=2.8.

Therefore,

Var[Y]=E[Y2]−E[Y]2=2.8−1.62=0.24.

Now, let's find Cov[X,Y]. We compute E[XY] using the rule of the lazy statistician:

E[XY]=∑(x,y)∈Sxy⋅f(x,y)=0⋅1⋅f(0,1)+0⋅2⋅f(0,2)+1⋅1⋅f(1,1)+1⋅2⋅f(1,2)=0+0+1⋅0.3+2⋅0.5=1.3.

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

Cov[XY]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=1.3−0.8⋅1.6=0.02.

Therefore,

Var[2X+3Y]=22⋅0.16+32⋅0.24+2⋅2⋅3⋅0.02=0.64+2.16+0.24=3.04.

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Combined Variance Given Some Moments
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ | $0.8$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =0.8-{0.8}^{2} \\  & =0.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.6 \\  & =1.6\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.6 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.6}^{2} \\  & =0.24.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We compute $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+1\cdot 1\cdot f(1,1)+1\cdot 2\cdot f(1,2) \\  & =0+0+1\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.3-0.8\cdot 1.6 \\  & =0.02.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X+3Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 0.16+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.24+2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 0.02 \\  & =0.64+2.16+0.24 \\  & =3.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

The joint probability mass function of the random variables X and Y is given below.

f Y=1 Y=2
X=0 0.1 0.1
X=1 0.3 0.5

Find Var[2X+3Y].

a
1.82
b
1.44
c
2.96
d
3.04
e
3.16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X and Y are random variables and a and b are constants, then

Var[aX+bY]=a2Var[X]+b2Var[Y]+2abCov[X,Y].

Also, the variance of a random variable X is determined by the formula

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2,

and the covariance of two random variables X and Y is given by the formula

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y].

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for X and Y. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

f Y=1 Y=2 fX
X=0 0.1 0.1 0.2
X=1 0.3 0.5 0.8
fY 0.4 0.6 1

Now, we can find Var[X]. If X is defined on a sample space SX, then

E[X]=∑x∈SXx⋅fX(x)=0⋅0.2+1⋅0.8=0.8

and

E[X2]=∑x∈SXx2⋅fX(x)=02⋅0.2+12⋅0.8=0.8.

Therefore,

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2=0.8−0.82=0.16.

Similarly, if Y is defined on a sample space SY, then

E[Y]=∑y∈Syy⋅fY(y)=1⋅0.4+2⋅0.6=1.6

and

E[Y2]=∑y∈Syy2⋅fY(y)=12⋅0.4+22⋅0.6=2.8.

Therefore,

Var[Y]=E[Y2]−E[Y]2=2.8−1.62=0.24.

Now, let's find Cov[X,Y]. We compute E[XY] using the rule of the lazy statistician:

E[XY]=∑(x,y)∈Sxy⋅f(x,y)=0⋅1⋅f(0,1)+0⋅2⋅f(0,2)+1⋅1⋅f(1,1)+1⋅2⋅f(1,2)=0+0+1⋅0.3+2⋅0.5=1.3.

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

Cov[XY]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=1.3−0.8⋅1.6=0.02.

Therefore,

Var[2X+3Y]=22⋅0.16+32⋅0.24+2⋅2⋅3⋅0.02=0.64+2.16+0.24=3.04.

Question 11

The joint probability mass function of the random variables X and Y is given below.

f Y=1 Y=2
X=0 0.1 0.1
X=1 0.3 0.5

Find Var[2X+3Y].

a
1.82
b
1.44
c
2.96
d
3.04
e
3.16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X and Y are random variables and a and b are constants, then

Var[aX+bY]=a2Var[X]+b2Var[Y]+2abCov[X,Y].

Also, the variance of a random variable X is determined by the formula

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2,

and the covariance of two random variables X and Y is given by the formula

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y].

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for X and Y. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

f Y=1 Y=2 fX
X=0 0.1 0.1 0.2
X=1 0.3 0.5 0.8
fY 0.4 0.6 1

Now, we can find Var[X]. If X is defined on a sample space SX, then

E[X]=∑x∈SXx⋅fX(x)=0⋅0.2+1⋅0.8=0.8

and

E[X2]=∑x∈SXx2⋅fX(x)=02⋅0.2+12⋅0.8=0.8.

Therefore,

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2=0.8−0.82=0.16.

Similarly, if Y is defined on a sample space SY, then

E[Y]=∑y∈Syy⋅fY(y)=1⋅0.4+2⋅0.6=1.6

and

E[Y2]=∑y∈Syy2⋅fY(y)=12⋅0.4+22⋅0.6=2.8.

Therefore,

Var[Y]=E[Y2]−E[Y]2=2.8−1.62=0.24.

Now, let's find Cov[X,Y]. We compute E[XY] using the rule of the lazy statistician:

E[XY]=∑(x,y)∈Sxy⋅f(x,y)=0⋅1⋅f(0,1)+0⋅2⋅f(0,2)+1⋅1⋅f(1,1)+1⋅2⋅f(1,2)=0+0+1⋅0.3+2⋅0.5=1.3.

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

Cov[XY]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=1.3−0.8⋅1.6=0.02.

Therefore,

Var[2X+3Y]=22⋅0.16+32⋅0.24+2⋅2⋅3⋅0.02=0.64+2.16+0.24=3.04.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X-Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.7 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =0.84.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =0.5-{0.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+2\cdot 0\cdot f(2,0)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1) \\  & =0+0+0+2\cdot 0.3 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.6-1.4\cdot 0.5 \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.84+(-1)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-1)\cdot (-0.1) \\  & =7.56+0.25+0.6 \\  & =8.41.\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X-Y].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.7 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.3+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.7 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =2.8-{1.4}^{2} \\  & =0.84.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =0.5-{0.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot f(0,0)+0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+2\cdot 0\cdot f(2,0)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1) \\  & =0+0+0+2\cdot 0.3 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.6-1.4\cdot 0.5 \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.84+(-1)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-1)\cdot (-0.1) \\  & =7.56+0.25+0.6 \\  & =8.41.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X+4Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ | $0.55$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.45+4\cdot 0.55 \\  & =2.2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.45+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.55 \\  & =8.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =8.8-{2.2}^{2} \\  & =3.96.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+4\cdot 1\cdot f(4,1)+4\cdot 2\cdot f(4,2) \\  & =0+0+4\cdot 0.2+8\cdot 0.35 \\  & =3.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =3.6-2.2\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X+4Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3.96+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =35.64+4+7.2 \\  & =46.84.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ | $0.55$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.45+4\cdot 0.55 \\  & =2.2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.45+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.55 \\  & =8.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =8.8-{2.2}^{2} \\  & =3.96.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+4\cdot 1\cdot f(4,1)+4\cdot 2\cdot f(4,2) \\  & =0+0+4\cdot 0.2+8\cdot 0.35 \\  & =3.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =3.6-2.2\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X+4Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3.96+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =35.64+4+7.2 \\  & =46.84.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13

The joint probability mass function of the random variables X and Y is given below.

f Y=1 Y=2
X=0 0.3 0.15
X=4 0.2 0.35

Find Var[3X+4Y].

a
 54.12
b
 43.86
c

d

e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X and Y are random variables and a and b are constants, then

Var[aX+bY]=a2Var[X]+b2Var[Y]+2abCov[X,Y].

Also, the variance of a random variable X is determined by the formula

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2,

and the covariance of two random variables X and Y is given by the formula

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y].

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for X and Y. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

f Y=1 Y=2 fX
X=0 0.3 0.15 0.45
X=4 0.2 0.35 0.55
fY 0.5 0.5 1

Now, we can find Var[X]. If X is defined on a sample space SX, then

E[X]=∑x∈SXx⋅fX(x)=0⋅0.45+4⋅0.55=2.2

and

E[X2]=∑x∈SXx2⋅fX(x)=02⋅0.45+42⋅0.55=8.8.

Therefore,

Var[X]=E[X2]−E[X]2=8.8−2.22=3.96.

Similarly, if Y is defined on a sample space SY, then

E[Y]=∑y∈Syy⋅fY(y)=1⋅0.5+2⋅0.5=1.5

and

E[Y2]=∑y∈Syy2⋅fY(y)=12⋅0.5+22⋅0.5=2.5.

Therefore,

Var[Y]=E[Y2]−E[Y]2=2.5−1.52=0.25.

Now, let's find Cov[X,Y]. We find E[XY] using the rule of the lazy statistician:

E[XY]=∑(x,y)∈Sxy⋅f(x,y)=0⋅1⋅f(0,1)+0⋅2⋅f(0,2)+4⋅1⋅f(4,1)+4⋅2⋅f(4,2)=0+0+4⋅0.2+8⋅0.35=3.6.

Cov[XY]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=3.6−2.2⋅1.5=0.3.

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Consider two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with expectations $\text{E}[X]=2,$ $\text{E}[Y]=4,$ mixed moment $\text{E}[XY]=10,$ and second raw moments $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=9$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=20.$ Find the variance of $2X-5Y.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =9-{2}^{2} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =20-{4}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =10-2\cdot 4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X-5Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot 5+(-5)^{2}\cdot 4+2\cdot 2\cdot (-5)\cdot 2 \\  & =20+100-40 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X-2Y].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.55+2\cdot 0.45 \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.55+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.45 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =1.8-{0.9}^{2} \\  & =0.99.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1)+2\cdot 2\cdot f(2,2) \\  & =0+0+2\cdot 0.2+4\cdot 0.25 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.4-0.9\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.99+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-2)\cdot 0.05 \\  & =8.91+1-0.6 \\  & =9.31.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1)+2\cdot 2\cdot f(2,2) \\  & =0+0+2\cdot 0.2+4\cdot 0.25 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.4-0.9\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.99+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-2)\cdot 0.05 \\  & =8.91+1-0.6 \\  & =9.31.\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |

| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ |

Find $\text{Var}[3X-2Y].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.5$ | $0.5$ | $1$ |

Now, we can find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.55+2\cdot 0.45 \\  & =0.9\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & ={0}^{2}\cdot 0.55+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.45 \\  & =1.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =1.8-{0.9}^{2} \\  & =0.99.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y},$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.5\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}{y}^{2}\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =2.5-{1.5}^{2} \\  & =0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ We find $\text{E}[XY]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}xy\cdot f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot f(0,1)+0\cdot 2\cdot f(0,2)+2\cdot 1\cdot f(2,1)+2\cdot 2\cdot f(2,2) \\  & =0+0+2\cdot 0.2+4\cdot 0.25 \\  & =1.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[XY] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =1.4-0.9\cdot 1.5 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 0.99+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 3\cdot (-2)\cdot 0.05 \\  & =8.91+1-0.6 \\  & =9.31.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
For three random variables ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3},$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]=3,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]=0.5,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{3}]=1.5\,
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=-0.75,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]=-3.5,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=4\,
$$

Find $\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}+6{X}_{3}].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}+6{X}_{3}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot 3+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{6}^{2}\cdot 1.5 \\  & +2\cdot 1\cdot 4\cdot (-0.75)+2\cdot 1\cdot 6\cdot (-3.5)+2\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdot 4 \\  & =3+8+54-6-42+192 \\  & =209.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 16
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Three Random Variables
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}+6{X}_{3}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot 3+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{6}^{2}\cdot 1.5 \\  & +2\cdot 1\cdot 4\cdot (-0.75)+2\cdot 1\cdot 6\cdot (-3.5)+2\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdot 4 \\  & =3+8+54-6-42+192 \\  & =209.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

For three random variables X1,X2, and X3, we have the following variances and covariances:

Var[X1]=3,Var[X2]=0.5,Var[X3]=1.5

Cov[X1,X2]=−0.75,Cov[X1,X3]=−3.5,Cov[X2,X3]=4

Find Var[X1+4X2+6X3].

a
217
b
196
c
185
d
224
e
209
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X1,…,Xn are random variables, and a1,…,an are constants, then

Var[∑i=1naiXi]=∑i=1nai2Var[Xi]+2∑i<jaiajCov[Xi,Xj].

Hence, for n=3 random variables, we have

Var[a1X1+a2X2+a3X3]=a12Var[X1]+a22Var[X2]+a32Var[X3]=+2a1a2Cov[X1,X2]+2a1a3Cov[X1,X3]+2a2a3Cov[X2,X3].

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

Var[X1+4X2+6X3]=12⋅3+42⋅0.5+62⋅1.5=+2⋅1⋅4⋅(−0.75)+2⋅1⋅6⋅(−3.5)+2⋅4⋅6⋅4=3+8+54−6−42+192=209.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Three Random Variables

decision.deviation_reason: Resolve uncertainty using the best supported response instead of an intentional error

solution.reasoning: The variance formula gives 3 + 4²(0.5) + 6²(1.5) + 2(1)(4)(-0.75) + 2(1)(6)(-3.5) + 2(4)(6)(4) = 3 + 8 + 54 - 6 - 42 + 192 = 209, option e. This is the intended algebraic response, but the premises are impossible: Cov[X₁,X₃]² = 12.25 exceeds Var[X₁]Var[X₃] = 4.5, and Cov[X₂,X₃]² = 16 exceeds Var[X₂]Var[X₃] = 0.75. Both violate the covariance inequality. The example's answer 209 concerns a different question and does not establish the current MA key.

question.name: Question 17
question.problem:
For three random variables ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3},$ we have the following variances and covariances:

$$
\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]=5,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]=4,\,\text{Var}[{X}_{3}]=2\,
$$

$$
\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]=3,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]=1,\,\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]=2\,
$$

Find $\text{Var}[3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3}].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3}] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 5+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+{4}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & +2\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 3+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =45+16+32+36+24+32 \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Three Random Variables
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},…,{X}_{n}$ are random variables, and ${a}_{1},…,{a}_{n}$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{X}_{i}]={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{i}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{i}]+2{\sum }_{i<j}{a}_{i}{a}_{j}\text{Cov}[{X}_{i},{X}_{j}].
$$

Hence, for $n=3$ random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[{a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3}] & ={a}_{1}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+{a}_{2}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+{a}_{3}^{2}\text{Var}[{X}_{3}] \\  & +2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]+2{a}_{1}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{3}]+2{a}_{2}{a}_{3}\text{Cov}[{X}_{2},{X}_{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3}] & ={3}^{2}\cdot 5+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+{4}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & +2\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 3+2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =45+16+32+36+24+32 \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 17
?

For three random variables X1,X2, and X3, we have the following variances and covariances:

Var[X1]=5,Var[X2]=4,Var[X3]=2

Cov[X1,X2]=3,Cov[X1,X3]=1,Cov[X2,X3]=2

Find Var[3X1+2X2+4X3].

a
205
b
165
c
195
d
175
e
185
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X1,…,Xn are random variables, and a1,…,an are constants, then

Var[∑i=1naiXi]=∑i=1nai2Var[Xi]+2∑i<jaiajCov[Xi,Xj].

Hence, for n=3 random variables, we have

Var[a1X1+a2X2+a3X3]=a12Var[X1]+a22Var[X2]+a32Var[X3]=+2a1a2Cov[X1,X2]+2a1a3Cov[X1,X3]+2a2a3Cov[X2,X3].

Substituting the given data into the formula above, we obtain

Var[3X1+2X2+4X3]=32⋅5+22⋅4+42⋅2=+2⋅3⋅2⋅3+2⋅3⋅4⋅1+2⋅2⋅4⋅2=45+16+32+36+24+32=185.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j+\frac{1}{1}\,k \\  & =i+j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i+j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{3}{y}^{2}=2x+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface z=sin⁡(xy)+y2 at the point (0,−1,1).

a
−x2=y+12=z
b
x=−y+12=z−12
c

e

EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: z=sin⁡(xy)+y20=sin⁡(xy)+y2−z

If we set f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(xy)+y2−z, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (0,−1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(0,−1,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,−1,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(sin⁡(xy)+y2−z)i+∂∂y(sin⁡(xy)+y2−z)j+∂∂z(sin⁡(xy)+y2−z)k=ycos⁡(xy) i+(xcos⁡(xy)+2y) j− k∇f(0,−1,1)=(−1)cos⁡(0) i+[(0)cos⁡(0)+2(−1)] j− k=−i−2j−k=⟨−1,−2,−1⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−0−1=y−(−1)−2=z−1−1x−1=y+1−2=z−1−1x1=y+12=z−11x=y+12=z−1

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

Question 3
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz), find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,1).

a
j+k
b
i+j+k
c
i+j
d
i+k
e
12i+j+k
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(1,1,1).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,1,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))i+∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))j+∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))k=1x i+1y j+1z k∇f(1,1,1)=11i+11j+11k=i+j+k

Therefore, i+j+k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,1).

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$
