Question 4
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface z=2x2+2y2+x at the point (12,1,3).

a
r=⟨3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
b
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,4,1⟩
c
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,−4,1⟩
d
r=⟨−3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
e
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

z=2x2+2y2+xz−2x2−2y2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=z−2x2−2y2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (12,1,3) can be found by computing ∇f(12,1,3).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (12,1,3):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(z−2x2−2y2−x)i+∂∂y(z−2x2−2y2−x)j+∂∂z(z−2x2−2y2−x)k=(−4x−1) i−4y j+k∇f(12,1,3)=(−4(12)−1)i−4(1) j+k=−3i−4j+k=⟨−3,−4,1⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(12,1,3) and passes through the point (12,1,3) can be written as

r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t∇f(12,1,3)=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface z=sin⁡(xy)+y2 at the point (0,−1,1).

a
−x2=y+12=z
b
x=−y+12=z−12
c
x=y+12=z−1
d
x=y+1=z−1
e
x=−y−1=z−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: z=sin⁡(xy)+y20=sin⁡(xy)+y2−z

If we set f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(xy)+y2−z, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (0,−1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(0,−1,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,−1,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(sin⁡(xy)+y2−z)i+∂∂y(sin⁡(xy)+y2−z)j+∂∂z(sin⁡(xy)+y2−z)k=ycos⁡(xy) i+(xcos⁡(xy)+2y) j− k∇f(0,−1,1)=(−1)cos⁡(0) i+[(0)cos⁡(0)+2(−1)] j− k=−i−2j−k=⟨−1,−2,−1⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−0−1=y−(−1)−2=z−1−1x−1=y+1−2=z−1−1x1=y+12=z−11x=y+12=z−1

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
question.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

a
i+2j+4k
b
4i−2j+4k
c
4j+k
d
−4i−2k
e
4i+j+4k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−1,2).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xy+5x+z2)i+∂∂y(xy+5x+z2)j+∂∂z(xy+5x+z2)k=(y+5) i+x j+2z k∇f(1,−1,2)=(−1+5)i+(1)j+2(2)k=4i+j+4k

Therefore, 4i+j+4k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

a
i+2j+4k
b
4i−2j+4k
c
4j+k
d
−4i−2k
e
4i+j+4k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−1,2).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xy+5x+z2)i+∂∂y(xy+5x+z2)j+∂∂z(xy+5x+z2)k=(y+5) i+x j+2z k∇f(1,−1,2)=(−1+5)i+(1)j+2(2)k=4i+j+4k

Therefore, 4i+j+4k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$
question.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1)$ can be found by computing

For the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz), find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,1).

a
j+k
b
i+j+k
c
i+j
d
i+k

12i+j+k
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(1,1,1).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,1,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))i+∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))j+∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))k=1x i+1y j+1z k∇f(1,1,1)=11i+11j+11k=i+j+k

Therefore, i+j+k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,1).

feedback.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j+\frac{1}{1}\,k \\  & =i+j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i+j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Question 4
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface z=2x2+2y2+x at the point (12,1,3).

a
r=⟨3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
b
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,4,1⟩
c
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,−4,1⟩
d
r=⟨−3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
e
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

z=2x2+2y2+xz−2x2−2y2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=z−2x2−2y2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (12,1,3) can be found by computing ∇f(12,1,3).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (12,1,3):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(z−2x2−2y2−x)i+∂∂y(z−2x2−2y2−x)j+∂∂z(z−2x2−2y2−x)k=(−4x−1) i−4y j+k∇f(12,1,3)=(−4(12)−1)i−4(1) j+k=−3i−4j+k=⟨−3,−4,1⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(12,1,3) and passes through the point (12,1,3) can be written as

r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t∇f(12,1,3)=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Question 4
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface z=2x2+2y2+x at the point (12,1,3).

a
r=⟨3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
b
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,4,1⟩
c
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨3,−4,1⟩
d
r=⟨−3,−4,1⟩+t⟨12,1,3⟩
e
r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

z=2x2+2y2+xz−2x2−2y2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=z−2x2−2y2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (12,1,3) can be found by computing ∇f(12,1,3).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (12,1,3):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(z−2x2−2y2−x)i+∂∂y(z−2x2−2y2−x)j+∂∂z(z−2x2−2y2−x)k=(−4x−1) i−4y j+k∇f(12,1,3)=(−4(12)−1)i−4(1) j+k=−3i−4j+k=⟨−3,−4,1⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(12,1,3) and passes through the point (12,1,3) can be written as

r=⟨12,1,3⟩+t∇f(12,1,3)=⟨12,1,3⟩+t⟨−3,−4,1⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

If we set f(x,y,z)=z−2x2−2y2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (12,1,3) can be found by computing ∇f(12,1,3).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (12,1,3):

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{3}{y}^{2}=2x+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,1).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the plane curve x3y2=2x+y. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (−1,1).

a
2x+y+1=0
b
3x+y+2=0
c
x−2y+3=0
d
x+y=0
e
x−y+2=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x3y2=2x+yx3y2−2x−y=0

If we set f(x,y)=x3y2−2x−y, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (−1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (−1,1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x3y2−2x−y)i+∂∂y(x3y2−2x−y)j=(3x2y2−2)i+(2x3y−1)j∇f(−1,1)=(3(−1)2(1)2−2)i+(2(−1)3(1)−1)j=i−3j=⟨1,−3⟩

Hence, ∇f(−1,1)=⟨1,−3⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (1,−3).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−(−1)1=y−1(−3)−3(x+1)=y−1−3x−3=y−13x+y+2=0

solution.reasoning: For F(x,y)=x³y²-2x-y, the gradient at (-1,1) is (3x²y²-2,2x³y-1)=(1,-3). This is a normal direction, so the normal line is y-1=-3(x+1), or 3x+y+2=0, option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}v(u-1)^{2} \\ v{u}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=v(u-1)^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=v{u}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1)v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2(u-1)v & (u-1)^{2} \\ 2uv & {u}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(u-1)v\cdot {u}^{2}-(u-1)^{2}\cdot 2uv \\  & =2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v(u-(u-1)) & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u(u-1)v=0$ defines the lines $u=0,$ $u=1,$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of $T,$ where $T$ is defined as 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+3{v}^{2} \\ u-2v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+3{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u-2v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

questions.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],

$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{2x}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{2x}{y} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3v}\end{aligned}

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-x+7y \\ x+3y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=-x+7y$ and $v(x,y)=3x-y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =7 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3-7\cdot 1 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Jacobian Determinants of Inverse Transformations
questions.raw_html:
5.Jacobian Determinants of Inverse Transformations?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[xyxy].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

H

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=v(u-1)^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=v{u}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1)v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2(u-1)v & (u-1)^{2} \\ 2uv & {u}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(u-1)v\cdot {u}^{2}-(u-1)^{2}\cdot 2uv \\  & =2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v(u-(u-1)) & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u(u-1)v=0$ defines the lines $u=0,$ $u=1,$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane.

Question 1
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[v(u−1)2vu2].

a
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and u=−v.
b
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0.
c
The critical points lie on the lines u=v and v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the lines u=v, and u=−v.
e
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and v=u.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=v(u−1)2 and y(u,v)=vu2.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2(u−1)v∂x∂v=(u−1)2∂y∂u=2uv∂y∂v=u2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2(u−1)v(u−1)22uvu2|=2(u−1)v⋅u2−(u−1)2⋅2uv=2u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=02u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v=02u(u−1)v(u−(u−1))=02u(u−1)v=0.

The equation 2u(u−1)v=0 defines the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0 in the uv-plane.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+3{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u-2v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

$$

$$

T:[uv]⟶[u2+3v2u−2v].

EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=u2+3v2 and y(u,v)=u−2v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2u∂x∂v=6v∂y∂u=1∂y∂v=−2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2u6v1−2|=2u⋅(−2)−6v⋅1=−4u−6v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0−4u−6v=02u+3v=0.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{2x}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{2x}{y} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3v}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=-x+7y$ and $v(x,y)=3x-y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =7 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3-7\cdot 1 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[−x+7yx+3y].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T.

a
4
b
−110
c

d

e
−12

EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=−x+7y and v(x,y)=3x−y.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=−1∂u∂y=7∂v∂x=1∂v∂y=3

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of T−1 is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|−1713|=(−1)⋅3−7⋅1=−10.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=−110.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

 
Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y} \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2v}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}v(u-1)^{2} \\ v{u}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=v(u-1)^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=v{u}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1)v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2(u-1)v & (u-1)^{2} \\ 2uv & {u}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(u-1)v\cdot {u}^{2}-(u-1)^{2}\cdot 2uv \\  & =2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v(u-(u-1)) & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[v(u−1)2vu2].

a
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and u=−v.
b
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0.
c
The critical points lie on the lines u=v and v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the lines u=v, and u=−v.
e
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and v=u.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=v(u−1)2 and y(u,v)=vu2.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2(u−1)v∂x∂v=(u−1)2∂y∂u=2uv∂y∂v=u2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2(u−1)v(u−1)22uvu2|=2(u−1)v⋅u2−(u−1)2⋅2uv=2u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=02u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v=02u(u−1)v(u−(u−1))=02u(u−1)v=0.

The equation 2u(u−1)v=0 defines the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0 in the uv-plane.

Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=v(u-1)^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=v{u}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1)v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2(u-1)v & (u-1)^{2} \\ 2uv & {u}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(u-1)v\cdot {u}^{2}-(u-1)^{2}\cdot 2uv \\  & =2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v.\end{aligned}

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$

$$

The equation $2u(u-1)v=0$ defines the lines $u=0,$ $u=1,$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[v(u−1)2vu2].

a
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and u=−v.
b
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0.
c
The critical points lie on the lines u=v and v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the lines u=v, and u=−v.
e
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and v=u.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=v(u−1)2 and y(u,v)=vu2.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2(u−1)v∂x∂v=(u−1)2∂y∂u=2uv∂y∂v=u2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2(u−1)v(u−1)22uvu2|=2(u−1)v⋅u2−(u−1)2⋅2uv=2u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=02u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v=02u(u−1)v(u−(u−1))=02u(u−1)v=0.

The equation 2u(u−1)v=0 defines the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0 in the uv-plane.

Critical points occur wherever this determinant vanishes: on the lines \(u=0\), \(u=1\), and \(v=0\). Thus option b is mathematically correct. feedback.html:
Question 1
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[v(u−1)2vu2].

a
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and u=−v.
b
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0.
c
The critical points lie on the lines u=v and v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the lines u=v, and u=−v.
e
The critical points lie on the lines u=0, and v=u.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=v(u−1)2 and y(u,v)=vu2.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2(u−1)v∂x∂v=(u−1)2∂y∂u=2uv∂y∂v=u2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2(u−1)v(u−1)22uvu2|=2(u−1)v⋅u2−(u−1)2⋅2uv=2u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=02u2(u−1)v−2u(u−1)2v=02u(u−1)v(u−(u−1))=02u(u−1)v=0.

The equation 2u(u−1)v=0 defines the lines u=0, u=1, and v=0 in the uv-plane.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of $T,$ where $T$ is defined as 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+3{v}^{2} \\ u-2v\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+3{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u-2v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+3{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u-2v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 6v \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2)-6v\cdot 1 \\  & =-4u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u+3v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u+3v=0$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[u2+3v2u−2v].

a
The critical points lie on the hyperbola u2−3v2=1.
b
The critical points lie on the line u=2v.
c
The critical points lie on the line 2u+3v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the line u=0.
e
The critical points lie on the line v=23.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=u2+3v2 and y(u,v)=u−2v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2u∂x∂v=6v∂y∂u=1∂y∂v=−2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2u6v1−2|=2u⋅(−2)−6v⋅1=−4u−6v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0−4u−6v=02u+3v=0.

The equation 2u+3v=0 defines a line in the uv-plane.

solution.reasoning: The Jacobian matrix is \(DT=\begin{pmatrix}2u&6v\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(-4u-6v=-2(2u+3v)\). Critical points occur where this determinant vanishes, so they lie on \(2u+3v=0\), option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

Question 2
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[u2+3v2u−2v].

a
The critical points lie on the hyperbola u2−3v2=1.
b
The critical points lie on the line u=2v.
c
The critical points lie on the line 2u+3v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the line u=0.
e
The critical points lie on the line v=23.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=u2+3v2 and y(u,v)=u−2v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2u∂x∂v=6v∂y∂u=1∂y∂v=−2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2u6v1−2|=2u⋅(−2)−6v⋅1=−4u−6v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0−4u−6v=02u+3v=0.

The equation 2u+3v=0 defines a line in the uv-plane.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{2x}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{2x}{y} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3v}\end{aligned}
$$

T−1:[xy]⟶[xyx2y].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
−vu
b
u3v
c
3v
d
−v
e
−13v
Submit
Correct

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=xy and v(x,y)=x2y.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=y∂u∂y=x∂v∂x=2xy∂v∂y=−x2y2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|yx2xy−x2y2|=y⋅(−x2y2)−x⋅2xy=−3x2y=−3⋅x2y=−3v.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=−13v

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[xyx2y].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
−vu
b
u3v
c
3v
d
−v
e
−13v
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=xy and v(x,y)=x2y.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=y∂u∂y=x∂v∂x=2xy∂v∂y=−x2y2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|yx2xy−x2y2|=y⋅(−x2y2)−x⋅2xy=−3x2y=−3⋅x2y=−3v.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=−13v

feedback.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{2x}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{2x}{y} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3v}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-x+7y \\ x+3y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=-x+7y$ and $v(x,y)=3x-y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =7 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3-7\cdot 1 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[−x+7yx+3y].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T.

a
4
b
−110
c
−15
d
14
e
−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=−x+7y and v(x,y)=3x−y.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=−1∂u∂y=7∂v∂x=1∂v∂y=3

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of T−1 is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|−1713|=(−1)⋅3−7⋅1=−10.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=−110.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=-x+7y$ and $v(x,y)=3x-y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =7 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3-7\cdot 1 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ \frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

 
Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y} \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2v}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}xy \\ \frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

 
Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y} \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2v}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[xyxy].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
−12v
b
2uv
c
−2u
d
12u
e
−2v
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1. Here, we have u(x,y)=xy and v(x,y)=xy.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=y∂u∂y=x∂v∂x=1y∂v∂y=−xy2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|yx1y−xy2|=y⋅(−xy2)−x⋅1y=−2xy=−2v.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=−12v

solution.reasoning: The inverse Jacobian determinant is y(-x/y^2)-x(1/y)=-2x/y=-2v. At non-critical points, the Jacobian determinant of T is its reciprocal, -1/(2v), so option a is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1** 

We plot the given points in the coordinate plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216627/assets/f329376e27ec08d2695db0e6d007e7a7b5342e7737c5d3f45eb524a2b1c2e572.png)

The distance between two points is the length of the line segment that connects them.

From the diagram, we see that the length of the segment is $3$ units, so the distance equals $3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216627/assets/66543bc73667ed70a965db4af2e657ad991660fc1b3a73a6e585943deffd3bbb.png)

**Method 2**

We can find the distance between the two points by finding the distance of each point from the $x$-axis and then subtracting.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216627/assets/5ded01b570e62d1e206aa8abd1012121367e60e749d441eb4e6ec7e3b12f6e8a.png)

The point $(0,5)$ is at a distance of $5$ from the $x$-axis, and the point $(0,2)$ is at a distance of $2$ from the $x$-axis. Therefore, the distance between the two points is $5-2=3.$

questions.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we can use the formula:

$$
\text{part}=\text{percentage}\times \text{whole}
$$

In our case, the whole is the weight of the first cake, which is $1,200\,\text{g}.$ The percentage is $140%,$ and the part is the weight of the second cake.

**Method 1**

First, we convert the percentage to a decimal:

$$
140%=140÷100=1.4
$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =140%\times 1,200 \\  & =1.4\times 1,200 \\  & =1,680\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $140%$ of $1,200$ is $1,680.$ So, the weight of the second cake is $1,680\,\text{g}.$

**Method 2**

First, we convert the percentage to a fraction:

$$
140%=\frac{140}{100}=\frac{140÷20}{100÷20}=\frac{7}{5}
$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =140%\times 1,200 \\  & =\frac{7}{5}\times 1,200 \\  & =7\times \frac{1,200}{5} \\  & =7\times 240 \\  & =1,680\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $140%$ of $1,200$ is $1,680.$ So, the weight of the second cake is $1,680\,\text{g}.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write $1\,\frac{1}{3}$ as an improper fraction:

$$
1\,\frac{1}{3}=\frac{(1\times 3)+1}{3}=\frac{4}{3}
$$

Since both fractions have the same denominators, we can combine them into one fraction, which gives

$$
\frac{2}{3}-\frac{4}{3}=\frac{2-4}{3}.
$$

Now, we work out $2-4$ using a number line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216627/assets/fd7fc3fedd2dbf8c90592bbedfdc15181eae63e4d2cbd71a4c036b2d75e8921c.png)

So, we get 

$$
\frac{2-4}{3}=\frac{-2}{3}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Since there are $18$ parrots and $15$ ducks, the ratio of parrots to ducks is $18:15.$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing both numbers by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,18 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,15 &  \\ \,\,\,↓÷\,\,3 &  &  &  & \,\,\,\,↓÷\,\,3 &  \\ \,\,\,6 &  & : &  & \,\,\,\,5 & \end{aligned}
$$

That means that $6:5$ is equivalent to $18:15.$ 

So, the complete statement is
"The ratio of parrots to ducks is $6:5\,$ because there are $6$ parrots for every $5\,$ ducks."

Therefore, the missing number is $5.$

14.Determining if a Number Is Divisible by 6?

Which of the following numbers are divisible by 6?

  1. 11289643

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.worked_solution:
A number is divisible by $6$ if it is divisible by both $2$ and $3.$

- The number $11\,289\,643$ is not divisible by $2,$ so it is not divisible by $6$ either.

- The number $13\,298\,784$ is divisible by $2,$ and it is also divisible by $3$ since the sum of its digits is divisible by $3:$

$$
1+3+2+9+8+7+8+4=42
$$

So, $13\,298\,784$ is divisible by $6.$

- The number $215\,153\,238$ is divisible by $2,$ and it is also divisible by $3$ since the sum of its digits is divisible by $3:$

$$
2+1+5+1+5+3+2+3+8=30
$$

So, $215\,153\,238$ is divisible by $6.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

feedback.worked_solution:
Since $5$ is larger than $1.2,$ the answer will be negative.

We start by solving an easier problem, which is to carry out the subtraction in the reverse order:

$$
5-1.2=3.8

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
1.2-5=-3.8.
$$

$$
12÷(-5)=-\boxed{}
$$

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $12$ by $5$ without any signs: $12÷5=\frac{12}{5}.$ Therefore, we get

$$
12÷(-5)=-\frac{12}{5}.
$$

a
 3 and 7
b
 7 and 3
c
 4 and 7
d
 4 and 3
e
 3 and 4

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[4(X-1)],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4},\, & 1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le {x}^{2}; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=4(x-1).
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le {x}^{2}\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215461/assets/bd8d2d36a0fe570e6ccdb096c6c39bc9c9edeed9b008dada504801025055438f.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4(X-1)] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}4(x-1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(x-1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{{x}^{2}}4(x-1)\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1){\int }_{1}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1)[y]_{y=1}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1)({x}^{2}-1)\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =3{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =3[(4-\frac{8}{3}-2+2)-(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+1)] \\  & =3(\frac{4}{3}-\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{11}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{(X+Y)}^{2}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4},\, & y\le x\le 4-y,\,0\le y\le 2; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}.
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 4-y,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215461/assets/8d1935944ffa0017da736fc540ff823df8a052c2c32c985553cde08ea5fce8da.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{(X+Y)}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}(x+y)^{2}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)^{2}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}(x+y)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}(x+y)^{3}]}_{x=y}^{x=4-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{1}{3}(4-y+y)^{3}-\frac{1}{3}(y+y)^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{\int }_{0}^{2}({4}^{3}-(2y)^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{\int }_{0}^{2}(64-8{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{[64y-2{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(128-32) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}xy,\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{y{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{3}{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{y}{4}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{8}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+2-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{X}^{3}(Y+1)],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\, & 1\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={x}^{3}(y+1).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le 2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}(Y+1)] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}{x}^{3}(y+1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}(y+1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{3}(y+1)\cdot \frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y(y+1){\int }_{1}^{3}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y(y+1){[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4y(y+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{4{y}^{3}}{3}+2{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & ={[\frac{4{y}^{3}}{3}+2{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{32}{3}+8)-(\frac{4}{3}+2) \\  & =\frac{46}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Find $\text{E}[{e}^{X-Y}],$ given that random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{y},\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={e}^{x-y}.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{e}^{X-Y}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}{e}^{x-y}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{x-y}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\cdot {e}^{y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{e}^{x}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(e-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[(e-1)y]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =(e-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=4(x-1).
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le {x}^{2}\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215461/assets/bd8d2d36a0fe570e6ccdb096c6c39bc9c9edeed9b008dada504801025055438f.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4(X-1)] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}4(x-1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(x-1)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{{x}^{2}}4(x-1)\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1){\int }_{1}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1)[y]_{y=1}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}(x-1)({x}^{2}-1)\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =3{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =3[(4-\frac{8}{3}-2+2)-(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+1)] \\  & =3(\frac{4}{3}-\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{11}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Suppose X and Y are continuous random variables, and f(x,y) is their joint probability density function. If r:R2→R is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

E[r(X,Y)]=∬R2r(x,y)f(x,y)dxdy.

In our case, we have

r(x,y)=4(x−1).

Now, let's sketch the region D={(x,y):1≤x≤2,1≤y≤x2}, where f(x,y) is nonzero.

Therefore, we obtain

E[4(X−1)]=∬R24(x−1)f(x,y)dxdy=∬D4(x−1)f(x,y)dxdy=∫12∫1x24(x−1)⋅34dydx=3∫12(x−1)∫1x2dydx=3∫12(x−1)[y]y=1y=x2dx=3∫12(x−1)(x2−1)dx=3∫12(x3−x2−x+1)dx=3[14x4−13x3−12x2+x]x=1x=2=3[(4−83−2+2)−(14−13−12+1)]=3(43−512)=114.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}.
$$

Now, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 4-y,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14215461/assets/8d1935944ffa0017da736fc540ff823df8a052c2c32c985553cde08ea5fce8da.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{(X+Y)}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}(x+y)^{2}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)^{2}\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}(x+y)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}(x+y)^{3}]}_{x=y}^{x=4-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{1}{3}(4-y+y)^{3}-\frac{1}{3}(y+y)^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{\int }_{0}^{2}({4}^{3}-(2y)^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{\int }_{0}^{2}(64-8{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{[64y-2{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(128-32) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability density function. If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that

$$
\text{E}[r(X,Y)]={∬}_{{R}^{2}}r(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonzero only in the rectangular region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{y{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{3}{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{y}{4}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{8}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+2-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find E[X2+Y2], given that random variables X and Y have the joint probability density function f(x,y)={xy,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2,0,otherwise.
